title: AI Financing Fears Spread From Equities Into Credit Spreads
content:
The window's defining move was AI anxiety migrating from stock valuations into the debt funding the buildout. Worries that hyperscalers and neoclouds are increasingly leveraged, and that capex may not pay off quickly, turned financing risk into the market's swing factor.

Stress built steadily. Semiconductors logged their longest losing streak since 2008, dragging the Nasdaq 100 lower as SK Hynix and Samsung slumped in a global tech rout. By late October global credit spreads reached a 17-month high near **129bp**, CoreWeave bonds traded at distressed levels with the stock off about **30%** from its October peak, and Oracle fell roughly **6.5%**.

Crucially, the wobble handed Treasuries a safe-haven bid, tightening the link between tech sentiment and rates. With leverage, not demand, now the vulnerability, **circular financing** among AI firms and hyperscaler debt loads stay the key risk into year-end.

title: Sticky Inflation Keeps a December Fed Hike in Play
content:
The higher-for-longer regime stayed the macro backbone. With the funds rate at **3.75%-4.00%** after September's hike, hot September CPI and PPI prints and core inflation near **3%** kept policy restrictive, and officials signalled another move was likely by year-end.

Markets converged on a hold at the late-October FOMC followed by a near-certain December hike, with economists almost unanimous. The 10-year Treasury yield hovered around **5%**, and a firm dollar — the DXY up almost **4%** from early-September lows — pushed towards multi-month highs before the AI-driven risk-off briefly eased yields.

The theme mattered because elevated discount rates pressured the richest equities, housing and credit, and kept the **term premium** alive in the long end. Incoming inflation data and the December decision remained the pivotal swing factors into year-end.

title: Middle East Supply Shock Lifts Crude to Six-Month Highs
content:
A Gulf **supply shock** ran hard through the window. Intensive tanker attacks around the Strait of Hormuz cut transit flows to roughly a third below normal, Houthi strikes hit Saudi energy infrastructure, and fears of renewed US or Israeli action against Iran stacked further risk onto an already tight market.

Prices climbed accordingly. Brent settled near **$117**, its highest in about six months and up over **3%** on the final session, while WTI closed around **$103**. Analysts flagged scenarios towards **$120** should the stand-off persist or Gulf exports be hit.

The rally mattered beyond energy: dearer crude fed directly into the hot inflation prints and hawkish rate rhetoric, reinforcing higher-for-longer. A durable recovery in Gulf flows would deflate the premium, leaving crude a key upside tail for inflation and a downside tail for risk.

title: Gold Consolidates Below Its Peak as Real Yields Bite
content:
Gold's pullback and consolidation became a cross-asset signal in its own right. After peaking near **$5,600** in January, bullion traded around **$4,100** through the window, pressured by multi-decade-high real yields and a firm dollar, slipping further as investors booked profit ahead of the Fed.

Yet the floor held. Central banks kept accumulating — official Q2 purchases ran near **290 tonnes**, up sharply year-on-year — and reserve diversification underpinned demand even as ETF investors trimmed, a classic **debasement hedge** against large deficits and geopolitical risk.

The tension between policy headwinds and structural buying mattered: it left gold range-bound rather than trending, a barometer of whether safe-haven demand can offset elevated rates. Its behaviour into year-end stayed a closely watched gauge of underlying investor anxiety.
